lede: Klara and Rosa are two AFs (Artificial Friends) in a city store, and at last it's their turn in the window. For an AF the window means three things: being seen, being chosen, and above all the Sun's 'nourishment'. On their fourth morning a taxi pulls up and out steps a thin girl who walks very carefully.

points.h: The first scene: touching a patch of sunlight
points.body:
The novel doesn't open with world-building but with a small moment. Boy AF Rex says the light on the floor can recharge them; Klara crouches to touch it just as it fades, and Rex calls her *greedy*.

The joke exposes a fear no AF admits: officially every model works anywhere, yet all of them feel weak after hours away from the Sun, and each suspects **the fault is only theirs**. Later a customer names Rex's model's 'solar absorption problems' to his face while he keeps smiling.

That is Ishiguro's method: **the cruellest things are said in the calmest voice**.

Klara speaks of *the Sun on his journey* and *his nourishment*. For her the Sun isn't a star but a being with a will, who can grant favours.

This is **the foundation of the whole book's faith**. Don't rush to call her wrong: she reasons from her own body's experience, much as the earliest human sun-worship did.

points.h: Klara's eyes: she sees much, says little
points.body:
In the window Klara is thrilled to see the outside whole: the RPO Building is made of bricks, pale yellow rather than white, twenty-two floors.

Watch for her habits, which recur throughout:
- **Estimating ages** to the half-year, and correcting herself.
- **Capitalised names** for things: *Beggar Man, Manager, the Tow-Away Zone sign, the Red Shelves*.
- **Her own words** for what she doesn't know: phones are *oblongs*, road workers are *overhaul men*.

Rosa, by contrast, stares at one sign and finds everything lovely. **Same model, very different curiosity.**

Some children look at the window with sadness or even anger. Manager explains that this is a special store and many children can't afford it. Klara adds that a child with no AF would surely be lonely; Manager pauses, then repeats *Lonely. Yes.*

That pause matters. AFs here are **expensive, owned by only some children**, and loneliness is the problem they exist to solve. The social background is laid down in chapter one.

points.h: Josie: a first conversation through glass
points.body:
Josie is pale and thin and walks as if checking each step is safe. She says she saw Klara from a taxi yesterday. Then she offers the most tempting promise you could make to a machine that worships the Sun:

> From up in my room you can see exactly where the Sun goes down.

Klara notes that when Josie smiles her face fills with kindness, and for the first time wonders whether Josie is one of the lonely children.

Josie's mother, about forty-five, has deep lines at her mouth and *a kind of angry exhaustion in her eyes*. Klara notices that when she reaches to touch her daughter's shoulder, **the hand hesitates in mid-air, almost withdraws**, and only then lands.

The gesture means nothing yet, and Klara doesn't explain it. Remember it.

Rosa asks why there are so few AFs on the street. Klara notices that AFs passing the store hurry and turn their faces away; she guesses embarrassment, then **fear** of being replaced by newer models.

The section ends with a girl striding ahead while her boy AF trails three steps behind, tired. Klara realises that **being bought is not the same as being loved**, and tells Rosa none of this.

expressions.en: Klara, that was greedy. You girl AFs are always so greedy.
expressions.zh: A teasing accusation that hides a real anxiety: AFs compete for the light they live on.

expressions.en: Unless you live in Alaska or down a mineshaft, you don’t need to worry.
expressions.zh: *down a mineshaft*: underground in a mine. A customer's breezy joke that dismisses a machine's deepest fear.

expressions.en: press their oblongs
expressions.zh: Klara's word for phones, from their shape. Her vocabulary is description, not brand names.

expressions.en: it was highly vulgar to make eye contact at such a moment
expressions.zh: *vulgar*: crude, in poor taste. Klara has learned human etiquette from watching.

expressions.en: a kind of angry exhaustion in her eyes
expressions.zh: Two feelings fused in one phrase. Klara reads faces with great precision, though she can't yet name the cause.

expressions.en: a kind of double taxi
expressions.zh: Two taxis so close they look like one vehicle: a child's way of seeing, and an image of things that seem one but are two.

questions: Klara believes the Sun is a 'he' with a will; Rosa hardly asks anything. Why might two AFs with the same design grow such different characters? Which seems the 'better' AF?
Manager says the sad children can't afford the store. What does this suggest about wealth and the status of AFs in this society?
The girl whose AF trails three steps behind, and Rex hearing his defect named aloud: what are these opening scenes preparing us to feel about 'being chosen'?

lede: Klara starts deliberately 'studying' human feelings she can't explain: taxi drivers fighting, an old couple reunited on the street. Josie returns to the window, this time with her mother staring at Klara. The window period ends and Manager doesn't praise them. Then a machine belching black smoke arrives in the street.

points.body:
Two taxi drivers get out and fight, their faces so twisted that a new AF might not recognise them as people. Rosa insists they're playing.

Klara does something remarkable: she tries **to find the starting point of that anger in her own mind**, imagining fighting Rosa. She can't, and laughs at herself.

Other feelings, she says, she later found some version of, *like the shadows made across the floor by the ceiling lamps*. That's her definition of her own emotions: **not the original, a shadow of it**.

points.h: Coffee Cup Lady and Raincoat Man
points.body:
After rain, an old man across the street waves frantically, while a small old woman (shaped like the upturned coffee cups on the store's shelves) stands still a long time before crossing. They embrace like one large person while the Sun pours nourishment on them.

Klara says they seemed happy, yet sad. Manager watches a long time and then says the key line:

> people feel a pain alongside their happiness

Klara immediately tests it on herself: if she met Rosa again years later, would she feel that? **She understands emotion by putting herself in the scene.** Notice, too, that Manager has probably lost someone.

points.h: 'I want to be straight with you'
points.body:
Josie's mother questions her daughter at length, then stands back, arms folded, staring. Josie explains: I told her I only want you, so she's checking you out.

Then Josie does something few children would: **before being chosen, she tells the bad news first**. She is sometimes unwell, things at home are unusual, and she won't lie as people do. What a sick fourteen-and-a-half-year-old cares about is whether **the other person comes willingly**.

Klara can't speak through the glass, so she uses gestures: a thumbs-up learned from a magazine, three and a half fingers for three and a half days, and finally her hands pressed together and shaken, borrowed from a taxi driver greeting a friend.

She means that whatever is difficult or frightening in Josie's house, they'll face it together. **Her whole promise fits inside a borrowed gesture.**

On the last day in the window Manager locks up without praising them. Klara steps down and the store **splits into ten boxes**: one shows Manager from waist to neck, one is almost all eyes (kindness and sadness), one is chin and mouth (anger and frustration).

This is the first of these 'boxed' views. They appear when Klara is under strain or facing **conflicting signals**, as if her processor must split the picture to handle it. They'll become more frequent.

points.h: The Cootings Machine: an enemy is born
points.body:
Road workers block half the street and bring a machine marked *Cootings*, three funnels pouring black smoke. For days the daytime turns dark, the sunlight vanishes from the floor, and Klara feels herself weakening.

Customers speak of *Pollution* (Klara capitalises it, like a proper noun); Rex says the machine exists to make it. In Klara's worldview it is **the Sun's enemy**. For now it's an episode, but remember the name.

expressions.en: like the shadows made across the floor by the ceiling lamps
expressions.zh: Klara's image for her own feelings: not sunlight but the shadows of lamplight. Modest and exact.

expressions.en: they were like one large person
expressions.zh: Two people holding each other so tightly they become one large person. A child's description, more concrete than 'embraced'.

expressions.en: people feel a pain alongside their happiness
expressions.zh: *alongside*: next to, together with. Not a blend like 'bittersweet', but two things side by side.

expressions.en: You never miss a thing, do you?
expressions.zh: A tag question that sounds like praise but carries a little unease: being seen through by a machine.

expressions.en: I detected there anger and frustration
expressions.zh: *detect*: an instrument's verb. Klara uses machine language, but what she reads is deeply human.

expressions.en: contrasting shades of gray were being displayed for selection
expressions.zh: She sees even smoke with shop eyes: displayed for selection, as she herself is.

questions: Klara calls her feelings 'shadows cast by ceiling lamps'. Do you think she has real feelings, or is she imitating? The book will keep asking.
Josie confesses her illness before being chosen; Klara promises with a borrowed gesture. What is this relationship built on from the start?
Manager's voice changes as she watches the reunion, and at the end she shows anger and frustration. What kind of person do you think she is?

lede: A girl with short spiky hair wants to buy Klara, and Klara plays dead wood. Manager covers for her but warns that children's promises rarely hold. Rosa is sold; in her second spell in the window Klara watches Beggar Man and his dog 'die and come back'. Then Josie really returns, and before paying, her mother asks Klara to do something strange.

points.h: A lapse: refusing to be bought
points.body:
The twelve-and-a-half-year-old girl likes Klara and tries to share secrets with her. Klara answers by **staring at the upturned coffee cups and letting her hand go limp**, like an unresponsive product. Manager notices and steers the father toward the new B3s.

Afterwards Manager says she won't do this again: *It’s for the customer to choose the AF, never the other way round.* Then the key question: do you believe you've made an arrangement?

Children promise everything at the window and most never come back. This is **the risk of loving a promise**, and the fear will return at the end of this section.

Rosa is bought without warning. Klara had expected time for a proper talk, to remind her about the Sun's nourishment. But Rosa is only excited: are the ceilings high? What colour is the car?

A **last smile over her shoulder**, and she disappears through the staff door. That's Rosa's exit. Recall Klara's question about meeting again years later, with pain alongside happiness.

Three B3s arrive, a more advanced model. An older boy AF helps them, but they **edge their feet away** so customers will see them as a separate group, exchanging glances.

Klara is puzzled: how could they be good AFs if their minds could invent ideas like these? This is snobbery among machines, and a hint: B3s may be cleverer but **less empathetic**.

points.h: Beggar Man and his dog: the Sun's special nourishment
points.body:
For a whole day Beggar Man and his dog lie motionless in a doorway; passers-by mistake them for rubbish bags. Klara is sure they're dead, sad, yet glad they died together.

The next day is bright, and Beggar Man sits up, stroking the dog. Klara concludes:

> a special kind of nourishment from the Sun had saved them

Readers will think they were frozen, drunk or asleep. For Klara it is **a miracle she has witnessed**. This is one of the book's most important seeds.

Moved to the rear alcove, Klara recognises Josie by her footsteps alone. Josie turns down a perfect B3, saying the AF she wanted must be gone.

Klara **doesn't step forward at once**: partly trusting Josie will come, partly afraid Josie will see her and choose someone else. Only when Manager helps does she walk into the light. Josie cries that she's still here; Klara answers: *We made a promise.*

The mother checks this isn't a B3, then asks what makes this one unique. Manager says: her appetite for observing and learning.

Then three questions: Josie's eye colour (grey), her voice's pitch (A-flat to C), the way she walks. Finally: **now walk like her.**

Klara does, blending the three times she has seen Josie walk. Midway she stops, because the mother's gaze passes **through** her, *as if I was the glass in the window*.

Why would a mother need a machine that can copy her daughter's walk? The book doesn't say. Put this beside the hesitating hand.

points.h: The last shot of Part One
points.body:
The mother says, 'Okay. We'll take her.' Josie hugs Klara, and over her head Klara sees Manager smiling **happily** while the mother, **grave**, searches her bag to pay.

One moment, three faces, three feelings. Part One ends.

expressions.en: It’s for the customer to choose the AF, never the other way round.
expressions.zh: *the other way round*: the reverse. Manager's rule, and the world's: AFs have no choice.

expressions.en: That you believe you’ve made an arrangement?
expressions.zh: *make an arrangement*: agree on something. Cool, commercial wording; for Klara it was a promise.

expressions.en: Children make promises all the time.
expressions.zh: The first lesson in human unreliability. Manager is warning Klara, and sympathising with the AFs who wait.

expressions.en: you could have mistaken them for the bags
expressions.zh: *mistake A for B*: take A to be B. Ishiguro writes poverty without adjectives, only by showing that others don't see it.

expressions.en: Her conversational voice has a range between A-flat above middle C to C octave.
expressions.zh: Klara describes a voice in musical pitch: machine precision, but also a very attentive kind of love.

expressions.en: as if I was the glass in the window
expressions.zh: Klara becomes transparent: the mother is looking through her at something far behind.

questions: Klara puts off one girl to wait for Josie, then hides out of fear. What do you make of these two very un-AF-like choices?
Klara believes the Sun revived Beggar Man. How would you explain it? Where might this belief lead her?
Why does the mother make Klara walk like Josie in front of everyone? What do you think she is looking at 'far behind the glass'?

lede: Klara arrives at Josie's house. Things in the kitchen keep 'changing their relationships', the housekeeper Melania dislikes her from day one, there's the mother's hurried morning coffee and the sunset from the bedroom's rear window. On her first trip outdoors Klara meets Rick, the neighbour boy flying mechanical birds, and Josie says the two of them will spend their lives together.

points.body:
Part Two opens with Klara learning something humans never find hard: **finding her way**. The kitchen's elements *would change their relationships to one another moment by moment*.

On the surface this is about space, but it's the book's method: Klara understands a home as a map that keeps rearranging itself, and so with relationships between people.

She names rooms: the Island, the Open Plan, the Button Couch. **Naming is how she settles in.**

Klara first assumes the housekeeper will be like Manager, leading to misunderstandings. She admits Melania *was opposed from the start to my presence*.

Melania's English is broken and blunt, and she calls Klara simply 'AF'. Don't hate her yet. Ishiguro is good at turning a character over slowly. Watch how she treats Josie.

Each morning the mother, in her high-rank work clothes, gulps a coffee; waking Josie in time is one of Klara's tasks.

One tender exchange: the mother misses Josie's colour drawings; Josie says her drawing in colour is like Mom playing that cello. *In fact, worse.* The mother laughs, and Klara notices the two smiles are identical.

On other mornings the mother stays tense. **The house's temperature depends on how Josie is that day.**

From the rear window Klara watches the Sun 'sink into the ground', and notices a dark box at the far end of the fields: Mr McBain's barn.

She seriously asks whether there's a gateway, or steps going into the earth. Josie jokes that the Sun would need a palace, minimum.

For Klara **the Sun has a resting place**. This barn will become the most important place in the second half. Remember her casual question.

Klara goes outside for the first time and meets a boy flying a flock of drone birds, two of which won't obey.

Rick is cold to Klara and keeps repeating *You said you’d never get one*. Josie rests both hands on his shoulder, as if to make him her height.

Klara's reply is graceful and shrewd: she hopes her presence will **never get in the way** of their friendship. Rick: a lot of things get in the way of friendships.

Here we first hear of 'the plan', and Josie mentions 'the other thing' Rick worries about. What it is emerges in the next section.

points.h: 'It's now my duty to be Josie's best friend'
points.body:
At sunset Josie calls Rick her best friend and Klara seems hurt: *it’s now my duty to be Josie’s best friend*.

Josie's answer is direct: *You’re my AF. That’s different.*

This line echoes through the whole book. Klara's love is real, but in Josie's world she remains a different kind of being.

expressions.en: its elements would change their relationships to one another
expressions.zh: Furniture that changes 'relationships' is an odd idea, and its oddness reminds you how Klara sees.

expressions.en: Me drawing in color is like you playing that cello.
expressions.zh: Josie's self-mockery: comparing her weakness to her mother's. Mother and daughter express closeness through jokes.

expressions.en: You’d think the Sun would need a palace, minimum.
expressions.zh: *minimum* at the end of a sentence means 'at the very least'. Common in speech: 'He needs two weeks, minimum.'

expressions.en: But Rick, well, we’re going to spend our lives together.
expressions.zh: *spend our lives together*: naive and certain at once, from a fourteen-year-old.

expressions.en: But a lot of things come in the way of friendships.
expressions.zh: *come in the way of*: obstruct. Rick means AFs, and something else he doesn't say.

expressions.en: Wind too strong! You want die up there or what?
expressions.zh: Melania drops 'to' and auxiliaries. A rude sentence whose content is worry for Josie.

questions: Klara says her duty is to be Josie's best friend; Josie says 'You're my AF. That's different.' What is the difference between these two relationships?
Klara seriously asks if there are steps into the earth near the barn. What do you make of her idea of the Sun? What does it remind you of in human history?
Rick says many things get in the way of friendship. Besides AFs, what do you think he means?

lede: Josie has to host an 'interaction meeting' for 'lifted' children and their mothers. In the hall the adults are overly polite about Rick and one slip mentions Sal, Josie's dead sister; in the Open Plan the children bait Rick and want to toss Klara across the sofa. The book's central social premise comes into focus.

points.body:
The adults greet Rick with a *strange caution*. One says it's *Such a shame a boy like that should have missed out*.

Missed out on what? The book never explains outright, but from here you can piece it together: children can be genetically 'lifted', lifted children get the good schools and futures, and Rick wasn't.

Ishiguro gives no manual, only **what people carefully don't say**.

The woman who slipped goes on: Josie will be grateful, you were so courageous. The mother asks quietly:

> Do you suppose Sal would want to thank me?

Silence. Someone else says *It’s our worst fear*.

Put it together: Sal was Josie's sister and is dead; Josie's illness is linked to being lifted; the mother made this decision for both daughters. It's the wound of her life, and nearly everything she does later must be read in its light.

In the Open Plan some girls are 'nice' to Rick: offering chocolates, asking what films he likes. Every question reminds him he doesn't belong.

Josie is hardest to watch. She first watches anxiously, then pushes Rick **with anger in her voice**, and later joins the girls' laughter.

Klara records Josie's hands: welcoming, offering, tense. **Josie becomes a different shape with different people.**

The boys want to 'test' Klara's coordination by throwing her, saying their B3s always land on their feet. Josie doesn't stop it, and even says *Now I’m starting to think I should have* (got a B3).

Klara's choice is striking: asked to sing, to greet, to describe what someone is wearing, she **doesn't respond**, staring at the bricks. She's waiting for Josie.

Rick rescues her by pointing at the small object in Danny's shirt pocket and asking if it's his *pet object*, embarrassing him in front of everyone.

Everyone goes outside, leaving Rick and Klara. Rick: *This is a meeting for lifted kids*; I don't belong.

He says he has to save Josie from this lot or she won't be Josie much longer. Klara says she'd like to help with their plan, since **they have similar goals**.

Klara sums up her lesson: Josie has 'changes', and she must be ready for them. An AF's lesson, and any loving person's.

expressions.en: Such a shame a boy like that should have missed out.
expressions.zh: *miss out*: lose an opportunity. No object needed; everyone knows what was missed. That's how this book works.

expressions.en: It’s our worst fear
expressions.zh: A stranger voices, for every mother in the room, the cost of lifting.

expressions.en: Some of us were lucky, some of us weren’t.
expressions.zh: Turning a choice into luck: comfort, and evasion.

expressions.en: It’s called conversation.
expressions.zh: A put-down formula, *It’s called + noun*, implying the other person doesn't even know that.

expressions.en: It couldn’t be you’re perhaps a little soft yourself, Danny?
expressions.zh: *soft*: weak, sentimental. Rick turns Danny's own insult on him: polite English with a blade inside.

expressions.en: I don’t belong here. This is a meeting for lifted kids.
expressions.zh: *belong*: who belongs where is a core question of the book, for Rick, for Klara, later for Josie.

questions: The book never defines 'lifted'; you assemble it from the adults' talk. What effect does this have on you?
Josie briefly sides with the girls, even saying she should have got a B3. How do you understand her?
Klara refuses to 'perform' and waits for Josie. Is this loyalty, pride or something else?

lede: Josie falls ill again. Her mother strikes a deal: get well by Sunday and we'll go to Morgan's Falls. Josie tips out old photos and Klara sees Sal for the first time. On Friday night the mother asks Klara if she's happy; on Sunday morning, with the engine running, the mother sees through Josie's pretence. Only the mother and Klara set off.

points.body:
The mother whispers: *So here’s the deal*. Get better by the weekend and on Sunday we go to Morgan's Falls.

Bargaining with a sick child is common, and cruel: **getting well becomes the child's responsibility**. Josie spends the next days proving she's fine, and the final morning's clash is buried in that one line.

Josie spills a box of photos on the rug and shows Klara herself as a little girl eating beside the waterfall. Klara asks who the other girl is.

Josie's face turns serious: that's Sal, my sister; she died. *It’s not like I miss her or anything.*

She says Sal had a different, worse illness. She may believe it, or it may be what adults told her. Come back to this after Part Four.

On Friday night the mother, drinking wine, calls Klara into the kitchen: Josie's fond of you, *so have I* become. Then: are you happy here? Do you miss the store?

Klara says sometimes, not often. The mother:

> It must be great. Not to miss things.

Half her face is in light, half in shadow. **She envies exactly what she herself can't do.**

Sunday seems fine; the mother even apologises for being harsh at breakfast. But once Josie is in the car the mother says *You think you have me fooled* — you're sick again.

The tension sits with Melania: told to help Josie out, she doesn't move, saying Miss Josie might make it. **The rude housekeeper sides, for the first time, with what Josie wants.**

Then the mother makes an unsettling proposal: Klara, stay in the car and come with me.

Klara tries to decline; the mother cuts in and challenges Josie: a moment ago you cared about Klara, now you don't want her to go? Josie gives in: go.

Klara says both the mother and Josie expressed the view that she should stay, so she stayed. That's AF logic: **carrying out human words literally**. Yet she saw Josie's face peering round the seat.

Next section, this decision casts a long shadow between them.

expressions.en: Worrying about you, Josie, that’s my work.
expressions.zh: *work* here means duty. The mother calls worry her job, then says Klara's too, putting them in the same role.

expressions.en: It’s not like I miss her or anything.
expressions.zh: *It’s not like... or anything*: a teenager's standard denial of feeling. The denial gives it away.

expressions.en: I don’t even know if that question makes sense.
expressions.zh: Having asked whether Klara is happy, the mother doubts the question itself. Does an AF have an inner life?

expressions.en: Not to be looking back all the time.
expressions.zh: *look back*: dwell on the past. She describes Klara and means herself.

expressions.en: You think you have me fooled, don’t you, girl?
expressions.zh: *have sb fooled*: have deceived someone. 'Girl', not 'honey': a cold form of address.

expressions.en: Maybe Miss Josie make it.
expressions.zh: *make it*: manage, get through. Melania's grammar is incomplete; her position is clear.

questions: The mother uses a 'deal' to promise the trip. Is it encouragement or pressure for Josie?
The mother envies Klara for 'not missing things, not looking back'. In light of Sal, how do you read this?
Klara says she stayed because both mother and daughter 'said so'. Did she really not see what Josie felt?

lede: Klara's first long car ride. On the way the mother says she envies Klara for having no feelings and mentions that Josie's father was 'substituted'. A bull by the path fills Klara with an almost cosmic dread. At the waterfall the mother ignores the view, stares at Klara and says: now you be Josie.

points.body:
After a long silence the mother says: *It must be nice sometimes to have no feelings. I envy you.*

Klara's reply is one of the best sentences in the book:

> The more I observe, the more feelings become available to me.

The mother laughs: then maybe don't be so keen to observe. This exchange is their basic difference: **the mother wants to feel less, Klara wants to feel more**.

A chemical plant appears in the distance. Josie's father was once a rising star there, until *He was…substituted*, like all the rest of them.

Replaced by what, by whom? Unsaid. But you can guess: in this world not only are children 'lifted', adults' jobs may be taken over by machines or something else.

Another premise **given in a single word**.

Climbing to the falls, Klara sees a bull in a field and is badly frightened. It makes her feel that some terrible error has been made, to let a creature so full of anger stand in the Sun's pasture.

This is the first appearance of **evil** in Klara's world: not human wickedness, but something that shouldn't exist. Remember the bull; it returns to her mind at her most vulnerable moments.

Holding her coffee, the mother stares at Klara as she once did from the sidewalk. Then she asks Klara to **be Josie**, just for a while.

Klara changes posture and voice: *Hi, Mom. Josie here.* The mother leans closer; in the boxes Klara sees joy, fear, sadness, laughter.

Then 'Josie' says something of Klara's own: I'll get better, *There’s special help coming*. The mother's face changes: *Who’s this talking?*

In this moment **Klara's faith and Josie's voice merge**, and even the mother can't separate them.

On the way back the mother has Klara sit in front and says they may do this again when Josie's too sick. Then: say nothing about this to Josie.

She presses: is your 'special help' a hope, or something you've seen that we haven't? Klara: only a hope, *But a real one*.

At home Josie, sketching on the rug, won't look up. Klara asks if they're still good friends. Josie: *You’re my AF. So we must be good friends, right?* There's no smile in her voice.

expressions.en: They always do this. Toy with your feelings.
expressions.zh: *toy with sb’s feelings*: play with someone's emotions. She means Josie, but says 'they': there was another child.

expressions.en: The more I observe, the more feelings become available to me.
expressions.zh: *become available*: become accessible. Klara treats feelings as something unlocked, mechanical yet moving.

expressions.en: Clean energy in, clean energy out.
expressions.zh: A verbless slogan, like advertising copy. The mother's verdict on the plant has an ironic edge.

expressions.en: No. That’s Klara. I want Josie.
expressions.zh: The mother instantly hears Klara's tone. She doesn't want company; she wants a stand-in.

expressions.en: What is this? Who’s this talking?
expressions.zh: She hears a stranger's belief come out of Josie's voice.

expressions.en: I suppose…it’s merely a hope. But a real one.
expressions.zh: *merely*: only. *a real one*: a genuine hope. The turn between the two is Klara's entire faith.

questions: The mother envies Klara's lack of feeling; Klara says observing gives her more feeling. Whose side are you on?
At the falls the mother has Klara 'be Josie'. What does she really want? What unsettles you here?
Is Josie's coldness at home jealousy, betrayal, or something else? Does she know what happened at the falls?

lede: The shadow of the falls trip hasn't lifted when Josie grows seriously ill. The mother's coffee moves to the bedroom; Melania sends Klara outdoors, where for the first time she stands alone by the fields thinking of the Sun and Beggar Man. The doctor comes less, Rick more: half an hour a day, during which he and Josie invent the 'bubble game'.

points.body:
Klara is puzzled: the humiliating interaction meeting left no shadow, but the falls trip, which she thought went well, keeps Josie cold. Even the mother's manner has changed.

Her reasoning implies **some shadows aren't cast by the event itself**. What matters to Josie is what happened while she wasn't there.

Melania, tired of Klara standing behind her, tells her *Go outdoors*. For the first time Klara stands alone at the fields, before a gate like a picture frame.

She thinks of Beggar Man and his dog, saved by the Sun's special nourishment. **Could the Sun cure Josie too?** The idea takes shape.

Note the rhythm: the book's most important plan begins on an idle afternoon when a housekeeper shoos her out of the house.

Rick is allowed thirty minutes a day. Klara says his visits fell into three phases: stiff, then relaxed, then... (next section).

Klara sits on the Button Couch facing the window, **watching them in the reflections**. Her usual position: present but turned away, seeing everything while pretending not to look.

Josie draws figures with empty speech bubbles; Rick fills them with what the people think or say.

It's a clever setup: **Josie supplies the surface, Rick the inside**. One person draws a shape; another imagines its thoughts. Much like what Klara must do: infer the inside from the outside.

Josie says Rick is jealous because he keeps bringing up her portrait: an artist in the city is doing it, and she has been to his studio four times.

Rick says he's not jealous but concerned. The man never shows her any sketches, only takes photos: *Everything you say about him sounds, well, creepy*.

Josie isn't bothered. Readers should be: **a portrait you are never shown** is one of Ishiguro's biggest plants.

expressions.en: AF. You behind me all the time. Creep me out. Go outdoors.
expressions.zh: *creep sb out*: give someone the creeps. Melania's verbs never change form, but her meaning is unmistakable.

expressions.en: Outside room, outside house, who care?
expressions.zh: Klara asks whether 'outdoors' means the room or the house; the housekeeper's impatience has some humour in it.

expressions.en: Who’s the artist here anyway?
expressions.zh: *anyway* at the end: 'after all'. Children squabbling.

expressions.en: I mean the way you keep bringing up my portrait.
expressions.zh: *bring up*: mention a topic. *keep doing*: do repeatedly.

expressions.en: He prefers photos because that way I don’t get exhausted
expressions.zh: Josie defends the artist. It sounds considerate; readers should be suspicious.

questions: Klara says the falls trip left 'shadows' and the meeting didn't. Why might that be?
In the bubble game Josie draws the outside and Rick writes the inside. How does the game relate to the book's themes?
What do you suspect about an artist who only takes photos and never shows sketches?

lede: The bubble game starts bringing fear instead of laughter. Josie draws an 'eyeball tribe' staring at a girl, and Rick refuses to fill the girl's bubble. Josie then needles Rick about his mother and 'society'; Rick writes something wounding on a drawing and stays away for days. Josie makes a new drawing and seals it in a large padded envelope.

points.body:
Josie draws a girl surrounded by people whose heads are like giant eyeballs, all staring. Rick says the creepier part is that *It looks like she wants them to keep staring*.

Josie calls that sick. But Rick may be seeing what Josie won't admit: **she fears the lifted kids' gaze, and wants it**.

Tidying up, Klara glimpses a sheet: a small figure between two 'nasties', and in its bubble Rick has written that the smart kids think it has no shape, but *I’m just keeping it hidden*.

Josie asks: does he think the small figure was him? Klara says he more likely thought it was Josie, and **was being kind**: reminding her not to lose herself among those people.

Josie bristles: who wants to be the same all the time? Later she says, *Maybe he did mean it to be kind*.

One rainy afternoon Josie asks why Rick's mother doesn't drive, why she has no 'society': *people take you seriously*.

Then the cruellest point: your mom didn't go ahead with you because she was scared. **She blames Rick's situation on his mother's choice.**

She urges him to try for Atlas Brookings, one of the few colleges that takes 'unlifted' students. Rick says the odds are under two percent.

Suddenly Rick writes on a drawing; Josie reads it: *I can’t believe you’d write this*.

Klara later sees it. In Josie's bubble Rick has written that she wishes she could run and skateboard and swim in lakes, but can't *because my mother has Courage* (capital C).

Remember the woman at the meeting praising the mother's courage? **Rick hands Josie's accusation straight back**: isn't your illness your mother's choice too?

Each child has named the other's deepest pain.

Rick doesn't come for days, and Josie grows listless. Klara suggests the bubble game; Josie says coldly that she shouldn't have.

One morning she makes a new drawing, has Klara fetch **a large padded envelope**, and pretends indifference. Klara guesses it's for Rick and offers to take it.

As she leaves, Josie asks: isn't it dull, living with a sick kid? Don't you wish you'd gone with someone else? Klara: my wish was to be Josie's AF, *And the wish came true*.

expressions.en: Am I to assume they’re aliens?
expressions.zh: *Am I to assume...?*: a formal English construction Rick likes, and gets teased for as 'too English'.

expressions.en: The smart kids think I have no shape. But I do.
expressions.zh: *shape*: form, here selfhood. Josie's 'shape' keeps changing throughout the book.

expressions.en: get into a taxi and people take you seriously
expressions.zh: *take sb seriously*: treat someone as important. Josie's definition of 'society', cold and exact.

expressions.en: Atlas Brookings may make a big thing of it
expressions.zh: *make a big thing of*: publicise heavily. Rick's clear-sightedness is sadder than Josie's optimism.

expressions.en: It must be dull, right? Living here with a sick kid.
expressions.zh: She jokes, but Klara sees fear beneath the smile.

expressions.en: Don’t take any shit from Rick.
expressions.zh: *take shit from sb*: put up with someone's nonsense (vulgar). Josie recovers her confidence in the most childish way.

questions: Rick writes 'I'm just keeping it hidden'. Klara calls it kind; Josie hears criticism. How do you read it?
Both children use the other's mother's choice as a weapon. Why do the children in this world care so much about that decision?
Josie asks Klara if she regrets choosing her. What is Josie really afraid of?

lede: Klara goes out alone for the first time, taking the envelope to Rick's house. It is cluttered; his mother's music blares upstairs. The drawing nearly makes Rick smile. Klara asks him to help her reach Mr McBain's barn, and then Miss Helen comes down: she wonders whether to treat Klara as a guest or a vacuum cleaner, tells a strange story about Sal, and asks Klara to help get Rick into college.

points.body:
Rick opens the envelope and looks a long time, almost smiling: the bubble reads 'Rick and Josie forever'. Klara calls it a kind picture.

But he won't simply go back. Josie keeps getting at him and then thinks a nice picture fixes it: *Things aren’t always that easily fixed*. He feels she's the one who should apologise.

Then something important: if Josie doesn't get better, *none of it will count*. The plan, the college, who was right, none of it.

Klara asks Rick to help her reach Mr McBain's barn. He assumes she wants to talk to Mr McBain about Josie. No, she says; she mustn't confide, or she'll risk the special help for Josie.

Her faith now has a rule: **the secret must not be spoken**. It holds to the book's last page.

Miss Helen appears, rummaging in a trunk for shoes: *Or do I treat you like a vacuum cleaner?*

She is elegant, odd, very English, unwell in body and mind, mocking, forgetful and sharp. At first sight she names Klara's position in this world: **a thing no one knows how to classify**.

points.h: The girl who came out of the grass
points.body:
Looking out of the window, Miss Helen says she once saw Chrissie (Josie's mother) come out of the grass holding a struggling child, and *The other one looked like Sal*.

Sal is long dead. Rick says his mother wasn't at her best that day; Miss Helen concedes she never meant it seriously.

The story is never explained. But set it beside 'the portrait' and you may feel an unease you can't name.

Miss Helen's real request: persuade Josie to make Rick try for Atlas Brookings. He won't go because he won't leave her.

Klara is surprised. She had thought humans always wanted to avoid loneliness:

> I didn’t think that humans could choose loneliness.

Sometimes there are forces stronger than that wish. Miss Helen will let her son go and be alone. **Another revision of Klara's idea of love.**

expressions.en: Be warned. It’s not fancy in here.
expressions.zh: *Be warned*: I should tell you. *fancy*: elaborate, smart. A self-deprecating English opener.

expressions.en: Or do I treat you like a vacuum cleaner?
expressions.zh: Placing an AF beside a vacuum cleaner: rude and honest. The world's attitude to AFs in one line.

expressions.en: The thought of all you robots receiving elocution lessons!
expressions.zh: *elocution lessons*: training in speech and pronunciation. Very English irony.

expressions.en: You can tear down a fence in a moment
expressions.zh: Looking at the fields: you can tear a fence down and put another up elsewhere. She isn't only talking about fences.

expressions.en: Especially, you see, since I have a secret weapon to help him.
expressions.zh: *secret weapon*: the weapon is a person, who appears in Part Four.

expressions.en: That there were sometimes forces more powerful than the wish to avoid loneliness.
expressions.zh: What Klara learns from Miss Helen: love can be stronger than the fear of being alone.

questions: Miss Helen asks whether Klara is a guest or a vacuum cleaner. What do you think Klara is in Josie's household?
How do you read Miss Helen's story of a child who 'looked like Sal'? Could it be connected to the portrait?
Klara learns that humans can choose loneliness. Do you agree with Miss Helen's choice?

lede: At dusk Klara crosses the fields alone toward the barn and nearly falls in the ditches; Rick, watching from his window, comes running and carries her. Inside, the barn is full of orange light. Sitting on a folding chair, Klara asks the Sun, in 'almost-words', to make Josie well, and offers a bargain.

points.body:
Klara has timed it to arrive as the Sun reaches the barn but before he rests. But the grass is tall and the ground uneven; she stumbles and feels the Sun is angry, that she *would soon fall into the ground*.

Then Rick parts the grass. From up there, he says, she looked like a fly buzzing on a window pane. Then: I'll carry you.

**A boy who says he doesn't understand any of this helps a machine fulfil her faith.** One of the book's gentlest images.

Close up, Klara has to admit it's an ordinary building, open on two sides, full of hay. The Sun's 'resting place' is humbler than she imagined.

She doesn't give up. She sends Rick home and goes in alone. Compare Josie's joke in Part Two that the Sun would need a palace.

points.h: Boxes and visions of the store
points.body:
The barn is full of orange light; hay particles drift like evening insects. Klara's vision splits into segments, and in them she sees **things from the store**: the Glass Display Trolley, the Red Shelves.

She remembers Manager, Rex calling her selfish, the bull, Rosa on the ground. Memory and sight mix.

Is this a visual malfunction, or something close to religious experience? Ishiguro deliberately won't say.

First the plea: *Please make Josie better. Just as you did Beggar Man.* Then she senses reluctance: the Sun can't yet see Josie apart from the humans who make Pollution.

She apologises, then bargains: I know how you hate Pollution, and I've seen the machine that makes it. If I could find it and destroy it, would you give Josie your special help?

**She is bargaining with a god.** An ancient way of praying, made especially moving in a machine's voice.

Afterwards the red glow softens and the segments fade. For the first time Klara walks to the back opening and sees the Sun sinking behind a line of trees, *smiling towards me kindly*.

Rick hasn't gone home; he waited. Klara says there is now reason for hope, and urges him to try for the college. Rick: Mum's obviously been working on you.

expressions.en: one of those flies that buzz around blindly on the window pane
expressions.zh: *buzz around blindly*: whirr about without direction. Rick apologises at once for being unkind; the joke eases the tension.

expressions.en: I wouldn’t guide you. I’ll carry you. Piggyback.
expressions.zh: *piggyback*: carried on someone's back. A childish word for the book's most solemn journey.

expressions.en: Please make Josie better. Just as you did Beggar Man.
expressions.zh: The simplest prayer, unadorned. *Just as*: in the same way as.

expressions.en: But Josie’s still a child and she’s done nothing unkind.
expressions.zh: Klara's defence: she's a child, she has done no wrong. A simple idea of justice.

expressions.en: Would you then consider, in return, giving your special help to Josie?
expressions.zh: *in return*: in exchange. Prayer turns into negotiation.

expressions.en: Just self-interest.
expressions.zh: Rick says he waited for selfish reasons: an English way of hiding kindness.

questions: Klara offers the Sun a bargain. Is this superstition, faith, or an expression of love?
Rick says he doesn't understand, yet carries her across the fields. Why does he help?
The store's shelves and trolley appear in the barn. How do you read these visions?

lede: Rick comes back; he and Josie grin at each other across the stairs, make up in the bedroom, and politely ask Klara to 'give privacy'. The mother announces a trip to the city to see the painter Mr Capaldi, and wants Klara to come. Melania pulls Klara aside: that painter is bad news, watch him. Late one night Josie cries from under the covers: I don't want to die.

points.body:
Rick, in the hall, looks up: he's heard a rumour they might be friends again. Josie, on the top step, gives her kindest smile.

In the bedroom Rick says he likes the room because it smells of Josie; she pretends outrage, laughing. They're glad they're not cross any more, and Rick puts his arms around her.

Klara says she always meant to give privacy, but there was concern about *hanky-panky*. Both burst out laughing. **A machine solemnly using that word is a rare comic moment.**

For days Klara thinks about how to find and destroy the Cootings Machine. She treats her promise to the Sun as **a concrete job**, a task to carry out.

She doesn't know where it is or how to destroy a machine. Her earnestness is touching and worrying.

The mother says she'll take Josie to the city next Thursday to finish the portrait at Mr Capaldi's, and **wants Klara with her when she goes in**: Mr Capaldi is fascinated by AFs and has questions.

The neighbours will ride along: Rick and Miss Helen have business in town. Rick tells Klara he's finally agreed to try for college, and even to meet his mother's 'old flame', who might pull strings.

On a rainy day Melania corners Klara: Ma'am won't let me go to the city but takes the AF. That Mr Capaldi is no good. *Paint portrait fuck.* Watch him.

She states the household's central truth: *Ma’am love Miss Josie. But Miss Sal die and mess Ma’am up bad.*

Klara says she has a plan to save Josie. Melania threatens to dismantle her if it makes Josie worse. Klara smiles at her for the first time. The housekeeper: *We same side*. **The hostile figure of Part Two has been on Josie's side all along.**

Late one night before the trip, Josie cries under her duvet for her mom. Klara says she's here, that's exactly her job. Josie: *I didn’t say you. I need Mom!*

The mother pushes Klara aside and holds Josie, who says: *Don’t want to die, Mom.*

Klara retreats to the dark landing. **Before the deepest fear, the AF is not the one who is needed.**

expressions.en: I heard this rumor we might be friends again.
expressions.zh: Making peace through 'a rumour' leaves both sides a way out.

expressions.en: The place smells of you, Josie.
expressions.zh: *smell of*: have the scent of. Klara has no sense of smell; this layer she can never share.

expressions.en: It’s just that there was concern about hanky-panky.
expressions.zh: *hanky-panky*: improper (often romantic) behaviour; slightly old-fashioned slang.

expressions.en: Ma’am love Miss Josie. But Miss Sal die and mess Ma’am up bad.
expressions.zh: *mess sb up*: damage someone emotionally. The most broken grammar delivers the most accurate diagnosis.

expressions.en: Okay, AF. We same side.
expressions.zh: *be on the same side*: Melania drops 'on' and 'are', but this is her greatest acceptance of Klara.

expressions.en: I didn’t say you. I need Mom!
expressions.zh: One line draws the boundary: however important Klara is, she is not the mother.

questions: Melania moves from hostility to 'we same side'. Rereading her in Part Two, do you see her differently?
The mother wants Klara with Josie at the painter's, and wants him to 'ask her questions'. What do you now suspect about the portrait?
Josie cries 'I need Mom, not you'. What does this moment mean for Klara?

lede: The city. At the triple window of the Friend's Apartment Klara watches for the father's taxi. Paul arrives late in a grey raincoat with a mirror that doesn't reverse your image. He and the mother clash at once; on the way to the painter's Klara recognises a street outside the car: her old store is gone.

points.body:
While watching for the father's taxi, Klara secretly hopes the Cootings Machine will pass. She admits the odds are small.

**At one window she waits for two things**: Josie's father and her own mission. That's Klara in Part Four: outwardly keeping company, inwardly executing a plan no one knows about.

The father greets Josie as *My favorite wild animal* and calls her 'animal' from then on. His gift is a mirror invented by a friend that shows you not reversed, but **as others see you**.

A telling gift: a substituted engineer gives his daughter a way to see her true appearance. One of the book's questions is exactly: **what is your real self?**

Josie asks him to say hello to Klara. He says only *Klara. Hello*, and the smile disappears. When the mother pushes him to say more, he retorts: *Part of the family. Is that what you’re saying?*

You don't yet know why. In 4·3 he'll explain.

In the car they argue. The mother is still grinding away at her law firm; the father urges her to let go: *I think the substitutions were the best thing that happened to me.*

He now lives in a 'community' with other substituted people. She thinks he's consoling himself; he thinks she's more bitter than he is. **Two readings of the same world.**

What they really want to fight about is the portrait. The mother: not here, not in this car.

Klara recognises the Tow-Away Zone sign: the very street she and Rosa watched. But there are no AFs, no Striped Sofa. Josie: maybe your store moved.

Klara has no time to think, because outside the car she sees **the Cootings Machine**. She says nothing, only smiles at Josie.

Josie promises they'll look for the store tomorrow.

expressions.en: Hey, Josie! My favorite wild animal!
expressions.zh: The father's pet name: odd and intimate, like him.

expressions.en: All these mirrors that show you the wrong way round?
expressions.zh: *the wrong way round*: reversed. The gift is also a metaphor about what's real.

expressions.en: Part of the family. Is that what you’re saying?
expressions.zh: A rhetorical question of doubt and displeasure: he won't accept Klara as family.

expressions.en: I think the substitutions were the best thing that happened to me.
expressions.zh: *the best thing that happened to me*: from a man who lost his career. Judge for yourself.

expressions.en: Not here you can’t! Not now and not in this goddam car!
expressions.zh: The mother's fury: she is fighting to keep a secret from Josie's ears.

questions: The father gives Josie a mirror that doesn't reverse. What might it symbolise in the book?
The father calls substitution the best thing that happened to him; the mother doesn't believe it. How do you see these two attitudes?
Klara spots the Cootings Machine and says nothing. What is she thinking?

lede: Mr Capaldi's studio is like a warehouse, with photo charts on the wall. The mother goes upstairs to see the 'portrait' and comes down pale. Klara is sent to do a 'survey', hears the father and the painter quarrel below, and quietly opens another door. Hanging behind it is Josie.

points.body:
Mr Capaldi seats Klara in a small cubicle: words and images on a screen, and she responds. It's just research, he says; make no special effort.

Below, the father and the painter argue: you're deliberately misconstruing me; there are always ethical choices.

You've probably guessed: **the survey tests how well Klara knows Josie**.

Klara opens the door, turns the corner of the L-shaped room, and sees Josie *suspended in the air*.

It isn't a painting or a sculpture but an AF with Josie's face and body, empty. Klara observes coolly and even offers professional advice: very accurate, *Though perhaps the hips should be a little narrower*.

**Funny and horrifying at once**: Klara is assessing another 'self' with a colleague's eye.

After the father leaves with Josie, the mother puts her face in her hands: maybe Paul's right, this whole thing's a mistake. She mentions *What we did with Sal*.

Capaldi: Sal is no comparison; what we made then was a doll.

Remember Miss Helen's child who 'looked like Sal': **after Sal died, the mother tried before**, and failed.

The mother says the real reason for today was Klara. Klara assumes she's to train the new Josie. Capaldi corrects her: *We’re asking you to become her*.

If the day comes, you'll inhabit that Josie with everything you've learned. Chrissie chose you as **the one best equipped to learn Josie**, until there's no difference between the first and the second.

Recall Part One: 'walk like Josie' in the store. Part Two: 'be Josie' at the falls. **They were all tests.**

Parked by the bridge, the mother hugs her: if you continue Josie you'll have me, and Rick too; we'll live away from everything.

Klara asks: and this body? The mother: *That’s just fabric*.

Klara answers calmly: until today I believed my duty was to save Josie, *But perhaps this is a better way*.

Has she agreed? Not entirely. Remember she still carries the Sun and the Cootings Machine inside her.

expressions.en: Henry, we don’t want Josie getting tired.
expressions.zh: She uses the painter's first name; their relationship goes deeper than client and artist.

expressions.en: I was an engineer, never a scientist.
expressions.zh: The father rejects being a 'fellow scientist': engineers build, scientists take apart. He draws a line.

expressions.en: Though perhaps the hips should be a little narrower.
expressions.zh: Klara's cool verdict. The book's blackest joke.

expressions.en: We’re asking you to become her.
expressions.zh: *become*: italicised in the original. Not imitate, not train: become.

expressions.en: Learn her till there’s no difference between the first Josie and the second.
expressions.zh: *learn sb*: unusual, since we normally learn a skill. Here a person is something to be learned.

expressions.en: What does it matter? That’s just fabric.
expressions.zh: *fabric*: cloth. The mother's verdict on Klara's body, cruel and offhand.

questions: When did you begin to guess the truth of the 'portrait'? Looking back, what clues were planted?
Capaldi says Klara can 'become' Josie. If it worked, would that be Josie?
The mother promises Klara 'you'll have me, and Rick'. Is she asking, bribing, or persuading herself?

lede: The father comes out of the burger place and takes the driver's seat beside Klara. He admits he's never been good with AFs, then asks: do you believe in the human heart? Klara asks him to drive to her old store's district; really she wants the Cootings Machine. They find it. Destroying it needs a certain solution, and Klara's body contains some.

points.body:
In the car he says *I’ve never been good at, well, relating to your kind*.

He asks whether Josie suspects the plan. Klara: the one in case she has to pass away? He thinks she may suspect but not dare look at it.

points.h: The heart as a house of many rooms
points.body:
The father asks: *Do you believe in the human heart?* Not the organ, the poetic sense. To truly learn Josie, you'd have to learn her heart.

Klara: it might be like a house with many rooms, but a devoted AF, given time, could walk through each.

The father: what if each room had another room inside, and another?

Klara holds that a heart, however complex, must be limited. **This exchange is the book's central argument.** Remember Klara's answer here; at the end she gives a different one.

Klara confesses: the store isn't the real reason. I need to find a machine and destroy it. It causes Pollution.

He can't see how this helps Josie; she can't explain: *Mr Paul has to trust me*. After a pause: let's at least give it a try.

Then a heavy line about hope: *Damn thing never leaves you alone*.

With the machine found, the father talks about Capaldi: I hate him because I suspect he's right, that there's **nothing unique about my daughter** that modern tools can't copy and transfer.

Chrissie is different; she'll never accept it. I have *a kind of coldness inside me she lacks*.

Read this against the mother's words at the falls: **a cold scientist and a hot-blooded mother**, both afraid of the same thing.

The father explains: the machine has a unit that P-E-G Nine solution would wreck. AFs carry some; a small incision near the ear could extract it. Your performance **shouldn't** suffer much.

Klara asks if he suggests this to damage her and sabotage Capaldi's plan. He admits the thought crossed his mind, but if he wanted to harm her there'd be easier ways.

Klara looks at the machine, masters her fear, and says: *Then let’s try.*

expressions.en: I’ve never been good at, well, relating to your kind.
expressions.zh: *relate to*: connect with, understand. *your kind*: distancing.

expressions.en: It might be like a house with many rooms.
expressions.zh: Klara's image: simple, concrete, confident.

expressions.en: Rooms within rooms within rooms.
expressions.zh: The father's rebuttal. The repetition itself enacts infinity: form becomes content.

expressions.en: Damn thing never leaves you alone.
expressions.zh: *leave sb alone*: stop bothering someone. Hope as a fly you can't swat away.

expressions.en: I have…a kind of coldness inside me she lacks.
expressions.zh: *lack*: be without. He treats his coldness as both a capacity and a flaw.

expressions.en: Then let’s try.
expressions.zh: Three words. Klara echoes his own phrase to accept a sacrifice of herself.

questions: The father says the heart is rooms within rooms; Klara says it must be limited. Whose side are you on?
The father hates Capaldi because he suspects Capaldi is right. How do you understand that hatred?
For a belief she can't explain, Klara lets someone drain fluid from her body. What does this remind you of?

lede: In the sushi cafe Klara's vision is blurred, because something is now missing from inside her. The father leafs through Rick's drone notebook; Miss Helen anxiously tells her son to 'act spontaneous'. Josie is unusually quiet. In the theatre crowd Klara's vision fragments, she hears her store has become a furniture shop, a woman says machines shouldn't take theatre seats, and Josie holds her tight: I'll never let anything bad happen to you.

points.h: A window she can't see through
points.body:
Klara can't see clearly out of the cafe window, not because of the glass but **because of herself**: since the extraction her sight has worsened. She tells no one.

She's still waiting for the Sun's response. The machine is destroyed; why hasn't he acted?

Josie insists she's fine, won't go back, won't talk. She tells Rick *Mom’s having one of her definitely weird days*.

What happened between her and her mother this afternoon? The mother later admits she told Josie the portrait wasn't a painting but a kind of sculpture, and **Josie remembers Sal's**.

Miss Helen keeps reminding Rick to make the meeting look accidental. She needles the father, implying his 'community' has fascist leanings; Rick apologises: she gets like this when anxious.

Outside the theatre the father says there are many ways to a successful life; Miss Helen says she is thinking ahead.

In the crowd the mother suddenly asks: *Do you regret it, Helen?* You know what I mean.

She means: **do you regret not lifting Rick?** Miss Helen doesn't answer, looking at the father and daughter. The mother says gently: it's okay.

The only time the two mothers speak directly of the decision. One gambled, one didn't, and neither knows if she was right.

A woman in a blue dress points at Klara: these seats are sought-after and shouldn't go to machines. *First they take the jobs. Then they take the seats at the theater?*

The book's only open hostility to AFs from a stranger. Josie says: Klara's my AF.

Then Josie embraces Klara and whispers *I’ll never let anything bad happen to you*. **She knows.**

expressions.en: Let’s just say for now Mom’s having one of her definitely weird days.
expressions.zh: *Let’s just say*: put it this way (without details). Josie protects Rick, and herself.

expressions.en: you must try and behave as though it’s spontaneous
expressions.zh: *spontaneous*: unplanned. Miss Helen asks her son to perform naturalness, a quiet echo of the book's theme.

expressions.en: this mess we’ve bequeathed to his generation
expressions.zh: *bequeath*: hand down to those who come after. The 'mess' is the whole world.

expressions.en: Do you regret it, Helen?
expressions.zh: 'It' is never named; both mothers know. Like 'missed out' in Part Two, the most important things go unsaid.

expressions.en: First they take the jobs. Then they take the seats at the theater?
expressions.zh: *First... then...*: a typical complaint pattern, echoing real anxieties about AI.

expressions.en: Don’t worry. I’ll never let anything bad happen to you.
expressions.zh: Josie's promise: now the human protects the machine.

questions: Klara loses part of her sight destroying the machine and tells no one. What do you make of this silent sacrifice?
The mother asks Miss Helen 'Do you regret it?' If you were Miss Helen, what would you say?
Josie holds Klara and promises to protect her. From what?

lede: Mr Vance chooses an empty, pie-shaped diner glowing yellow. He leafs through Rick's notebook asking ethical questions, then abruptly turns. Miss Helen says yes, we are asking for a favour, and twenty-seven years of grievances come out one by one. Rick says he wants no help at all. That night Josie tells Klara her mother proposed an 'idea'. On the drive home the next day Klara sees a second Cootings Machine.

points.body:
The diner is shaped like a slice of pie, its point at a fork in the road, the only light in the dark. No other customers, yet every table is set; Klara thinks the Diner Manager is **a lonely man**.

In the last chapter this diner will merge, in Klara's overlapping memories, with the waterfall and the dark-sky morning.

Vance studies Rick's drone designs: these birds gather data; couldn't criminals, paramilitaries or cults use them? Rick says ethical issues are for legislators. Vance: *That’s well said*.

He is courteous until Miss Helen speaks. **His courtesy is a way of waiting for her.**

Miss Helen says: yes, we are asking you for a favour. Vance: *Twenty-seven years’ worth of a problem*.

They shared a life for five years and she left. At a party she humiliated him over a report he hadn't read; there was a voicemail he still hears.

She apologises point by point. Vance: *Once you were a kind of queen, Helen*, and thought you could do whatever you liked.

Watching his mother humiliated, Rick finally says he wants no help. Miss Helen cries that he doesn't know what he's saying.

Vance leaves. Miss Helen wonders: *if that was enough*. Will it satisfy him?

She understands what he wanted: **not an apology but her humiliation**, a price she'll pay for her son.

At night Josie tells Klara her mother offered to quit her job and stay with her. Klara says if that would make Josie less lonely, she'd step aside. Josie: I'm not lonely. Klara: *Perhaps all humans are lonely*.

Driving home, Klara sees by a tall building a **New Cootings Machine** pouring grey mist. Now she knows why the Sun hasn't acted: the Pollution goes on.

Her head drops. Josie notices: see, Mom, you've upset Klara too.

expressions.en: Just somewhere we can sit down, look at one another and talk.
expressions.zh: Vance's reason for the diner: 'look at one another' means him and Helen, not Rick.

expressions.en: But in the end, it’s for legislators
expressions.zh: *legislator*: lawmaker. Rick hands ethics to others, and Vance is pleased.

expressions.en: Twenty-seven years’ worth of a problem.
expressions.zh: *... years’ worth of*: treating time as a measurable quantity, loaded with grievance.

expressions.en: Once you were a kind of queen, Helen.
expressions.zh: *a kind of*: a sort of. Vance's resentment still holds deep admiration.

expressions.en: I’m wondering if that was enough. If that will satisfy him.
expressions.zh: Miss Helen's clarity: she knows this was a transaction.

expressions.en: Perhaps all humans are lonely. At least potentially.
expressions.zh: *potentially*: possibly, in principle. Another of Klara's conclusions about humans, closer and closer to the ending.

questions: Did Vance want an apology or humiliation? Why is Miss Helen willing to bear it?
Rick says he wants nothing. Is he protecting his mother or his own dignity?
Klara discovers a second Cootings Machine. Does her bargain still count?

lede: Eleven days after the city, Josie truly begins to fail. In the grass Rick confronts Klara: you kept saying there was hope. Klara asks him to carry her to the barn once more, and to answer a question: is the love between you and Josie real? In the barn, the Sun's face is reflected in seven panes of glass. Days later, on a morning dark with storm clouds, the Sun comes out.

points.body:
Josie's breathing turns strange, her eyes open but empty; the doctor no longer smiles. In the grass Rick tells Klara she spoke as if there were a special reason: *So you had me hoping too*.

Klara admits she hesitated after the city, hoping help would come anyway. Now she decides to **go back and explain in person**.

Klara says she needs something extra to plead with. Tell me truthfully: is your love for Josie genuine and lasting?

Rick doesn't need to think: we grew up together, *we’re part of each other*; we have our plan; our love is genuine and forever, and lifting makes no difference.

He means it now. Remember this; the last chapter returns to it.

The barn glows orange again, but the hay blocks are lower, the store's Red Shelves crooked, the coffee cups gone. Klara apologises: I failed; I didn't foresee a second machine.

She says she doesn't mind losing precious fluid and would give it all. She also confesses she now knows 'the other way' to save Josie, but isn't sure it would work.

Then a new argument: **favouritism** may be undesirable, but if the Sun makes exceptions, the most deserving are young people who will love each other all their lives.

Glass sheets lean in a corner. The Sun's reflection lies on them, and Klara sees not one face but **seven superimposed**: the outermost forbidding, the next more unfriendly, those beyond softer and kinder, the last perhaps humorous.

Together, *a single face, but with a variety of outlines and emotions*.

This is nearly Ishiguro's answer about the heart: not one room, not endless rooms, but **many layers forming one face**.

Six days later the sky grows strangely dark after breakfast, and the wind rises. The mother calls Rick into the kitchen and asks if he feels like the winner: Josie gambled high; you played safe, and *what you’ve won is small and mean*.

Rick passes on Josie's message: she loves you, and if she could do it again she'd choose exactly as you did.

Then Klara sees outside: the Sun is coming out! They rush upstairs, where Melania is cursing and pulling the curtains; Klara cries: open them, open everything! The Sun falls on Josie in *a ferocious half-disc of orange*. Josie wakes: what's with this light?

expressions.en: So you had me hoping too.
expressions.zh: *have sb doing*: cause someone to keep doing something. Rick's accusation holds disappointment and fear.

expressions.en: Josie and I grew up together and we’re part of each other.
expressions.zh: *be part of each other*: a young person's most certain definition of love.

expressions.en: Hundred percent I will.
expressions.zh: Spoken 'a hundred percent', article dropped. Rick's promise is clean and immediate.

expressions.en: I know favoritism isn’t desirable.
expressions.zh: *favoritism*: unfair preference. The same word Vance used in Part Four: Klara asks the Sun for a kind of string-pulling.

expressions.en: a single face, but with a variety of outlines and emotions
expressions.zh: *a variety of*: many different. Seven faces making one: one of the book's final images of a person.

expressions.en: You played for low stakes and what you’ve won is small and mean.
expressions.zh: *play for high/low stakes*: bet big/small. The mother uses gambling language for her most painful choice.

expressions.en: Go away, damn Sun!
expressions.zh: Melania fears the glare will hurt the patient. She and Klara, one shutting out the light and one letting it in, both act for Josie.

questions: In her second plea Klara says she doesn't mind losing the fluid and confesses 'the other way'. Why does she think the Sun needs to know this?
The Sun's reflection is seven superimposed faces. How do you read this image, and how does it differ from the father's 'rooms within rooms'?
Was Josie saved by the Sun, or did she recover by chance? Which do you think Ishiguro wants us to believe?

lede: Josie recovers and grows from a child into an adult. The grass is cut and the barn stands out sharply. Rick and Josie head toward different futures; their love back then, he says, was no lie. Mr Capaldi returns wanting to study Klara, and the mother sends him away: let her have her slow fade. Josie hugs Klara before leaving for college. Finally, in a yard of discarded things, Klara meets Manager again.

points.body:
Part Six opens: the Sun's special nourishment worked for Josie as it did for Beggar Man, and *she grew not only stronger, but from a child into an adult*.

Time suddenly speeds up; seasons and years pass in a few lines. Mr McBain cuts the grass in all three fields, and the barn looks taller and more sharply outlined. **With the mystery mown away, the barn is just a barn.**

Rick, driving a car called the Wreck, sees Josie less and less. He asks Klara whether that morning had something to do with her. Klara won't say, for fear the help will be taken back.

She worries: you said your love was genuine, and now you prepare different futures; will the Sun feel deceived? Rick: *that was the truth at the time*. Out there, he'll always keep searching for someone like her.

Sitting in the Yard, Klara finally lets go: perhaps the Sun already knew they'd meet again after many years, like Coffee Cup Lady and Raincoat Man.

points.h: The Utility Room and a high window
points.body:
When Josie's friends visit, Klara waits in the Utility Room upstairs. Josie opens the door, stacks a trunk and a crate into two steps so Klara can see out of the high small window.

*I know how much you love looking out.*

A small act, but it shows Josie still **remembers who Klara is**.

Mr Capaldi comes, heavier and greyer. There's growing backlash against AFs, people afraid they've become too clever, and he wants to open Klara up to study her.

The mother steps in front of Klara: *Klara deserves better. She deserves her slow fade.*

The mother's greatest kindness to Klara, and the best ending this world offers an AF: **not to be taken apart, only forgotten**.

Before driving off to college Josie hugs Klara: you may not be here when I get back; *You’ve been just great*. Klara thanks her for choosing her. Josie: *No-brainer*.

The car goes over the hill. What happens next is not described; we simply find Klara in **the Yard**, a field of discarded things, sitting on hard ground, unable to move, a construction crane in the distance.

points.h: The special thing wasn't inside Josie
points.body:
Manager, collecting little souvenirs at the Yard, finds Klara. Klara says she could have continued Josie if necessary, but doesn't think it would have worked: not for lack of accuracy, but because something would have stayed beyond her reach.

Then the book's answer:

> There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie.

It was inside those who loved her. Capaldi was searching in the wrong place.

This answers the father's 'rooms within rooms', and the whole book: **what makes a person irreplaceable is not how complex they are inside, but how others love them**.

Klara tells Manager the Sun was always kind to her, once especially. Manager: I'm sure he has been. They look at the Sun together.

Manager drags the crate back and walks off. She walks differently now, leaning left every second step. Halfway she stops, and Klara thinks she'll look back. She doesn't; she gazes toward the distant crane, and walks on.

The book's last image: **one forgotten figure watching another walk away**.

expressions.en: she grew not only stronger, but from a child into an adult
expressions.zh: *not only... but...*: one sentence spans several years.

expressions.en: that was the truth at the time
expressions.zh: *at the time*: then. Four words resolve the conflict between 'love changes' and 'love was real'.

expressions.en: I know how much you love looking out.
expressions.zh: Josie remembers that Klara loved the window in the store: grown-up Josie's gift.

expressions.en: Klara deserves better. She deserves her slow fade.
expressions.zh: *fade*: dim, wane. What the mother wins for Klara is a quiet death.

expressions.en: No-brainer.
expressions.zh: *no-brainer*: an obvious choice. Josie answers Klara's weightiest thanks with a light word.

expressions.en: I have my memories to go through and place in the right order.
expressions.zh: *place in order*: arrange. Klara's last work is sorting her memories.

expressions.en: It was inside those who loved her.
expressions.zh: The book's answer, in seven words.

questions: Rick says their love was real then, and parting now isn't a lie. Do you agree? Would the Sun feel deceived?
The mother says Klara deserves her 'slow fade'. Is this kindness or abandonment?
Klara concludes that the special thing was in those who loved Josie. Are you convinced? What does it mean for Klara herself?
